scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The walkaround began in the 1840s as a dance for one performer in blackface minstrel shows, expanding by the 1850s to involve full troupes.
Scholars note its origins as a parody of the ring shout, a religious dance of African plantation slaves tracing back to West African traditions.
Over time, minstrel troupes wrote dedicated walkaround compositions like 'Dixie', and the dance eventually incorporated the cakewalk.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Functions as a stage finale for the first half of a minstrel show, leading into intermission.
It served as a caricature of sacred slave ring shouts while functioning as a vehicle for competitive vernacular dance.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers start seated in a semicircle.
At the onset of fast 2/4 or 4/4 music, they stand and clap or slap their bodies ('patting Juba').
Individual dancers or couples step downstage to the center of the semicircle, performing elaborate steps for roughly 16 bars.
Watch for Patting Juba, Downstage Solo.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (hpNdQDWgy7I)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers begin seated in an opening semicircle, move downstage to the focal point for solos, and break ranks across the stage for the finale.
